content: HAT medium, which stands for Hypoxanthine-Aminopterin-Thymidine medium, is a specialized selection medium used in mammalian cell culture. It functions by combining aminopterin, a drug that inhibits folate metabolism by targeting the enzyme dihydrofolate reductase, with hypoxanthine and thymidine, which are intermediates in DNA synthesis. Hypoxanthine is a purine derivative, while thymidine is a deoxynucleoside. Aminopterin blocks the de novo synthesis of DNA, a process essential for cell division. However, the presence of hypoxanthine and thymidine in the medium allows cells to bypass this blockage through the salvage pathway, provided they possess the necessary enzymes. This means that only cells with functional copies of the genes encoding these enzymes can survive and proliferate in HAT medium. The enzyme dihydrofolate reductase, which catalyzes the reduction of dihydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate (THF), is specifically inhibited by aminopterin. THF plays a critical role in transferring single-carbon units to specific targets in the cell. One such target is thymidylate synthase, an enzyme that converts deoxyuridine monophosphate (dUMP) into thymidine monophosphate (TMP). TMP can then undergo further phosphorylation to form thymidine triphosphate (TTP), one of the four nucleotide precursors required by DNA polymerases for DNA synthesis. Without THF, the conversion of dUMP to TMP cannot occur, halting DNA synthesis unless TMP is supplied from an alternative source. In HAT medium, thymidine serves as this alternative source. Cells can absorb thymidine from the medium and convert it into TMP through the action of the enzyme thymidine kinase (TK). Similarly, the synthesis of inosine monophosphate (IMP), a precursor to guanosine monophosphate (GMP) and guanosine triphosphate (GTP), also requires THF. This pathway can also be bypassed in HAT medium. Hypoxanthine, absorbed from the medium, is converted into IMP by the enzyme hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRT) via the salvage pathway. The use of HAT medium in cell culture thus acts as a form of artificial selection, favoring cells that possess functional TK and HGPRT enzymes. This selective pressure can be further refined using specific drugs. For example, cells lacking TK are resistant to bromodeoxyuridine (BrdU), while cells lacking HGPRT are resistant to 6-thioguanine (6-TG) and 8-azaguanine. Selection with one of these drugs, followed by incubation in HAT medium, can yield revertant colonies. HAT medium is widely used in the production of monoclonal antibodies through a process known as hybridoma technology. In this method, B cells are fused with HGPRT-negative, immortalized myeloma cells using agents such as polyethylene glycol or the Sendai virus. The resulting fused cells are incubated in HAT medium. Aminopterin in the medium blocks the de novo nucleotide synthesis pathway, causing unfused myeloma cells to die, as they cannot produce nucleotides via either the de novo or salvage pathways. Unfused B cells also die due to their limited lifespan. Only the hybrid cells, which combine the antibody-producing capability of B cells with the immortality of myeloma cells, survive. The surviving hybrid cells are then diluted into multiwell plates so that each well contains a single cell. The supernatant from each well is tested for the desired antibody. Since the antibodies in a given well are produced by the same B cell, they are specific to a single epitope and are referred to as monoclonal antibodies.
